question: Your team runs Claude Code with the -p flag in CI to extract API reference entries, such as HTTP method, path and auth requirement, from route handlers in many services. Each field gets a confidence score. Entries whose fields all score above a threshold are published to the internal developer portal without review, and the rest go to reviewers. A tech lead proposes that reviewers also check a stratified random sample of the published high-confidence entries every week, drawn from each service and field. What is the main benefit of this proposal?

options.text: It measures the ongoing error rate of the published high-confidence entries in each service and field, and it can reveal new error patterns that no existing check targets.
options.reason: The guide uses stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to measure their ongoing error rate and to detect novel error patterns.

options.text: It lets the team drop the field-level confidence scores, because reviewers who check a random sample of entries no longer need a score to decide which entries to publish.
options.reason: The guide keeps calibrated field-level confidence scores to route review attention. Sampling measures errors among high-confidence outputs and does not replace these scores.

options.text: It lets the team stop routing low-confidence entries to reviewers, because the weekly sample of published entries now covers all of the review work that the pipeline will need from now on.
options.reason: The guide still routes low-confidence or ambiguous extractions to human review. Sampling the high-confidence entries adds to that routing and does not replace it.

options.text: It produces one combined accuracy figure for all published entries across every service, which is the clearest single number for deciding whether to lower the threshold.
options.reason: The guide warns that one aggregate accuracy figure can hide poor performance in specific segments. Stratifying the sample exists to show the error rate of each segment.
